A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cognitive deficits seen in ALS are associated with abnormal activity in the anterior thalami and in the anterior and medial prefrontal cortices.

we have shown that in some patients with ALS, there are abnormalities of function in the anterior cingular gyrus and in the parahippocampus, and these are correlated with abnormalities in verbal fluency and in the performance of a motor task.

there is a correlation between the degree of cognitive impairment (as measured by the verbal fluency test) in ALS patients and the amount of activation of a network that includes the anterior thalamus, the parahippocampus, the anterior cingulum and the medial prefrontal regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain regions that are involved in the generation of movement are not the same as the ones that are involved in planning and executing a movement.
the brain is very complex and there are a lot of different ways that the brain is affected in ALS.
